how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Attic insulation bid calculator

How much should I charge for blown-in attic insulation?

Enough to cover the bags the R-value delta actually buys, not enough to match the cheapest postcard on the block. An attic already at R-30 going to R-38 is not the same job as the same attic sitting at R-13 going to R-49, and a flat price per square foot cannot see the difference.

Open the free bid calculator

Price the inches, then the bags

Start with length × width on each attic section. Write down the existing R — depth times the product already in the bays, or a measured inch count converted with that product’s R-per-inch — and the target R the homeowner asked for. Inches to add equal the difference divided by the R-per-inch of the bag you will blow. Cubic feet equal area times those inches divided by 12. Bags equal that volume rounded up to the settled yield printed on the bag. Cellulose, blown fiberglass, and mineral wool are different truckloads.

Air sealing is not “included”

A blow on top of leaky penetrations is a photo for the homeowner, not an R-value they will feel. Each can light, plumbing stack, and wire hole is foam and time. Baffles at the eaves keep the soffit open and keep the blow from choking the intake. A hatch without a dam becomes a snowdrift in the hallway. If those lines are “included” in a $1.50-a-foot special, they are unpaid.

Vaulted ceilings and removal are a second labor list

Loose-fill does not belong on a cathedral ceiling. Count that area so the homeowner sees why it is not in the bag count, then bid dense-pack or foam separately. Wet, compressed, or the wrong product is removal plus a dumpster, not a free upgrade. Contractors who quote only the blow and “figure the rest in” are guessing the line that most often blows a postcard special.

Then load the wage and keep a margin

A blower paid $32 often costs more than $41 once employer taxes, respiratory workers’ compensation, liability, and paid time off are counted. Overhead sits on top of that direct cost. Margin is a share of the price the customer sees, not a markup you add last and forget. The walk-away number is total cost: below it the job makes nothing, even before you pay yourself.

This is not an energy-code price list

This is not a manufacturer coverage chart, not an energy-code requirement, and not a finding that an attic is airtight, permitted, or rebate-eligible. The starting R-per-inch, bag yields, and hours are ballpark numbers so a contractor can see the shape of a bid. Replace them with the bag you buy and times from your own jobs, confirm measurements on site, and have a qualified professional review anything that has to be signed, inspected, or rebated.

Price this job in the calculator

Common questions

How much should I charge for blown-in attic insulation?

Charge the bags and hours the job will actually take — attic floor area times the inches implied by target R minus existing R, divided by the cubic feet you get from a bag, plus air-sealing penetrations, baffles, travel, and a dumpster if you are pulling existing fill — then divide cost by one minus your target margin. A flat price per square foot hides the difference between topping R-30 to R-38 and taking R-13 to R-49.

How many bags of insulation do I need for an attic?

Bags come from volume, not floor area. Inches to add equal (target R minus existing R) divided by the product's R-per-inch. Cubic feet equal area times those inches divided by 12. Divide by the settled cubic feet printed on the bag you actually buy, and round up. Cellulose, blown fiberglass, and mineral wool have different yields, so the same attic is a different truckload.

Is this an energy-code price list?

No. Starting R-per-inch, bag yields, and hours are editable ballpark numbers, not a manufacturer coverage chart, an IECC climate-zone table, or a finding that any attic is airtight, permitted, or rebate-eligible. Confirm measurements and product charts on site.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a manufacturer, energy-code, rebate, or insurance inspection. Verify every figure against your own costs and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

FOR INSULATION CONTRACTORS

Bid the bags, not the attic.

Bags come from the R-value delta, not the floor area. An attic already at R-30 going to R-38 is not the same truckload as the same attic sitting at R-13 going to R-49, and a flat price per square foot cannot see the difference. Price the areas, the product, the air sealing, and the baffles — then see the walk-away number before a $1.50-a-foot special eats the week.

How much should I charge for blown-in attic insulation?

This calculator vs. a flat price-per-square-foot special

The attic

One row per section. Length × width is the floor. Existing R and target R decide the inches — and the bags. Check vaulted when that section cannot take loose-fill; it stays in the area split but buys nothing.

The job

R-per-inch and bag yield follow common product charts as a time-and-material budget you can edit — not a manufacturer coverage table, an energy-code requirement, or a finding that any attic is airtight, permitted, or rebate-eligible. Deeper fills multiply blow hours on that section because the bags have to be hauled and raked.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, respiratory workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. A blower paid $32 often costs more than $41 in the attic. Underestimating that is how a $1.50-a-foot special loses money.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the attic area goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting R-per-inch, bag yields, and hours are common ballpark numbers, not a manufacturer coverage chart, an energy-code table, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them. This is not a finding that any attic is airtight, permitted, or rebate-eligible.

    Common questions

    What does this insulation estimate include?

    The price adds up blown-in bags from the R-value you need to add across each attic area, baffles, air-sealing parts for each penetration, an optional removal-and-haul line for existing insulation, a chosen add-on kit, a dumpster when removal is selected, setup and travel time, a trip fee, overhead, and your target margin — all from the areas, product, and rates you enter, not a flat price list.

    Why does bag count come from the R-value gap instead of the floor area?

    Bags are driven by how many inches need to go in, which is the target R-value minus what is already there, converted through the product’s R-value per inch. An attic already at a high R-value going up a little is a smaller truckload than the same square footage starting low and going to the same target, even though a flat per-square-foot price would charge them the same.

    Does it handle vaulted ceilings and areas already at or above target?

    Yes. A vaulted area is counted in the total attic area shown but is excluded from bags and blow hours, since it is not being topped up. An area already at or above its target R-value adds zero bags and zero blow hours for that area as well — both still appear in the takeoff so you can see they were considered.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Usage counts are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and a share link encodes only the quote fields in the page’s URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.

    What’s the difference between the quote price and the walk-away price?

    The quote price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, the trip fee, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — bags, baffles, air sealing, removal, labor, and the trip — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all.

    Does this check energy codes, manufacturer coverage charts, or rebate eligibility?

    No. This is not a manufacturer, energy-code, rebate, or insurance inspection. R-value per inch, bag yield, and blow hours are ballpark shop figures you can replace with your own product’s coverage chart; whether a job qualifies for a utility rebate or meets a local energy code is a separate question this tool does not answer.

    How is this different from a paid platform like FieldCamp?

    FieldCamp is a paid job-management platform for scheduling crews and running job costing across every job an insulation business does. This calculator connects to nothing: you price one attic in your browser, with no account to make, cancel, or pay for. See this calculator vs. FieldCamp for which job fits which situation.

    Why not just quote a flat price per square foot?

    Because two attics of the same square footage can need a different truckload of bags, depending on the R-value delta and whether air sealing or removal is part of the scope. See this calculator vs. a flat price-per-square-foot special for where a per-foot rate usually gets it wrong.

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Attic Insulation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price-per-square-foot special

"$1.50 a foot" is not a price for an attic — it is a price for one specific R-value delta, product, and scope, quietly applied to every attic that walks in the door.

What a flat per-foot rate is

A flat rate is the fastest way to quote: multiply the attic's square footage by a number and read off a price. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and crews use it because it needs no takeoff. It is also the rate a customer holding a postcard or a competitor's website will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one job — one product, one starting R-value, one target, no removal, no unusual penetrations — and then reused for every attic afterward, whether or not the next attic looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each attic section's area, existing R-value, and target R-value, the product's R-per-inch and bag yield, the air-sealing penetrations and baffles, and your loaded labor and overhead. It converts the R-value delta into inches and bags per section, adds the blow, air-seal, and removal hours separately, and returns a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this attic, not a generic one.

What a flat per-foot rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the attic is going from R-30 to R-38 or from R-13 to R-49 — a several-times difference in bags for the same floor area. Converts each area's existing-to-target R-value into inches added, then bags, from the product's own R-per-inch and cubic feet per bag.
Prices "the attic" as one blow, with no separate line for penetrations, a hatch dam, or baffles at the eaves. Times air sealing at minutes per penetration and baffles at their own rate, so that labor shows up instead of being absorbed into the blow or skipped.
Assumes a clean blow over existing material, so a job needing removal of wet or contaminated fill gets quoted the same as one that does not. Adds removal hours per square foot plus a dumpster line only when that scope is turned on, so the two jobs price differently.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so the labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the crew a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price, the effective hourly rate, and how much of labor is air sealing versus blowing, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get attic insulation wrong?

Because bags come from how much R-value has to be added, not from the floor area alone. An attic already at R-30 going to R-38 needs a fraction of the fill that the same square footage at R-13 going to R-49 needs. A flat rate charges both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

Air sealing and baffles. Foam at penetrations, a hatch dam, and baffles at the eaves are their own hour stack separate from the blow itself, and a rate built around "square feet of attic" has nowhere to put that labor. Crews who price off the blow alone and figure sealing in for free are short before the truck leaves the yard.

What happens when the existing fill has to come out first?

A flat installed rate assumes a clean blow over existing material. Wet, settled, or rodent-contaminated fill means removal hours plus a dumpster before a single bag goes in, and a rate that never asked the question charges the same price for a job that takes twice as long.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same product, same starting R-value, same target, no removal — a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard rate does not know which band a given attic is in and neither does the crew until they measure it.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, bag prices, or what competitors charge. It takes the wage, bag cost, and overhead you enter and turns them into a walk-away price for the areas, R-values, and scope you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat rate per square foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

← Attic Insulation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. FieldCamp

Both end with a bag count and a price, built on opposite assumptions about what you are willing to install and pay for.

What FieldCamp is

FieldCamp is a paid job-management platform aimed at insulation and other field-service businesses: schedule crews, estimate and send jobs, invoice, and track cost and profit across every job the business runs, on an ongoing subscription. It is built to run day-to-day operations for a company doing many jobs, not to price a single attic once.

Getting there means creating an account and paying an ongoing subscription priced by users and features.

What this calculator is

This page does not schedule anything and keeps no account. You open it in a browser, type an attic's square footage, existing R-value, target R-value, and bag yield, and it shows the bag count and walk-away price for that one job. Close the tab and it is gone unless you save a share link or print a proposal — there is no crew schedule, no invoicing, and no subscription.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to schedule crews, estimate, and invoice every job my insulation business runs, and track cost against each one. FieldCamp or a comparable paid platform — ongoing job management is exactly its job, and this calculator has no schedule or invoicing.
I have one attic to bid right now and want the bag count and walk-away price before a flat-rate special goes out. This calculator — type the R-value delta and square footage, get a price, no account.
I do not want to create an account or start a subscription to price a single job. This calculator — nothing to sign up for.
I want the tool to remember every job I have bid and compare estimated to actual material cost over time. FieldCamp or a comparable paid platform — this calculator has no job list and no memory between visits beyond what your own browser keeps.

Neither tool is the wrong choice in general. An insulation company scheduling crews and running many jobs a season is the case a paid platform is built for. A single attic, priced once against a flat-rate special before the bid goes out, is the case this page is built for.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or FieldCamp?

They fit different points in the job. FieldCamp is a paid job-management platform built for insulation and field-service businesses: schedule crews, estimate jobs, invoice, and track costs across every job a company runs, on an ongoing subscription. This page does one thing: you type an attic's square footage, existing and target R-value, and bag yield into a browser, and it shows a bag count and a walk-away price for that one job, right now, with no account and no subscription. If you want a platform that schedules crews and runs job costing for an ongoing insulation business, that is what FieldCamp is built for. If you want to price one attic before a square-foot special goes out, this page does that with nothing to sign up for.

Is this page affiliated with FieldCamp?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by FieldCamp. FieldCamp is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

This page is a factual comparison of what each tool does, not an evaluation of which is better. Details about FieldCamp above describe the general shape of the product as publicly described at the time of writing and may have changed — verify against FieldCamp's own site before deciding.
